Reproducibility, parity and the materials datasheet

Source: vignettes/reproducibility-and-parity.Rmd
reproducibility-and-parity.Rmd

A stimulus set is usually described rather than shared. The methods section says the words were matched on length and frequency, and the set itself, the criteria that produced it and the code that applied them are not recoverable from the paper. lexsync treats the set as an artefact in its own right: the selection and the trial order are deterministic, the R and Python engines produce the same artefacts from the same input, and each run emits a provenance record with the checksums needed to verify it.

This vignette explains the guarantee and its limits, the mechanisms that achieve it, the continuous-integration test that keeps it honest, and the two records a run leaves behind.

library(lexsync)
schema <- yaml::read_yaml(
  system.file("extdata", "schema.yaml", package = "lexsync")
)
lex <- load_lexicon(
  system.file("extdata", "en_example.csv", package = "lexsync"),
  schema, language = "english"
)
pool <- build_pool(lex, list(length = c(3, 7), frequency = c(3.8, 7.0)))

design <- list(
  name = "vignette_repro", language = "english", n_per_condition = 15,
  conditions = list(
    list(name = "high", define_by = list(frequency = c(5.2, 7.0))),
    list(name = "low",  define_by = list(frequency = c(3.8, 4.4)))
  ),
  match_on = list("length", "n_density", "old20"),
  counterbalance = list(lists = 1)
)

What is guaranteed

The claim is worth stating exactly. Given the same lexicon and the same design, the R and Python engines produce byte-identical stimuli under the standardised_euclidean and joint matching methods, under continuous selection, and under both pseudoword generators. The claim covers which items are chosen, how they are paired and the order they are presented in, so the generated experiments are byte-identical in full. The only exceptions are the mahalanobis and optimal matching methods.

‘Byte-identical’ is meant literally, and stating it that way turned out to matter. The parity test originally read both engines’ stimuli files back with a CSV parser and compared the values, under which 1 and 1.0 are the same number. On that test 13 of the shipped designs passed while differing byte for byte. Three of the differences were serialisation: a whole number written 1 by one writer and 1.0 by the other, a boolean written FALSE and False, and a small value written 9e-4 and 0.0009. One was not: two reported means differed in the last decimal published, because one engine’s summation was pairwise and the other’s was not. Every sum in the package now goes through a single compensated-summation algorithm written out in both engines, whose agreement follows from IEEE-754 requiring addition and subtraction to be correctly rounded, and the mean, variance and standard deviation are built on it. The median sorts and takes the middle value, or the plain-double average of the two middle values when the count is even, which keeps it clear of the long-double accumulator that stats::median() reaches by way of mean(). The artefacts are now compared as bytes.

Two files sit outside the claim by design, because each records the engine that produced it: the materials datasheet names its engine and that engine’s package versions, and the run log adds wall-clock timestamps. Their contents are compared field by field instead.

Within one engine, selection is a pure function of its input.

a <- match_stimuli(pool, design, schema)
b <- match_stimuli(pool, design, schema)
identical(a, b)
[1] TRUE

That is not a small claim to make about an R function. Repeated calls agree because nothing in the selection path consults a random number generator, and because every operation that could depend on the ambient environment has been pinned. The interesting question is why the Python engine also agrees, since the two implementations share no code.

How byte-identical output is achieved

Cross-engine identity is not an accident of two careful translations. Each mechanism below closes a specific way the engines could otherwise drift.

The first is that there is no random number generator anywhere. The obvious way to choose 15 items from 700 is to sample them, and lexsync never does. The anchor condition is chosen by an even spread across its sorted subpool, taking positions along the whole range, and every later item is determined by a distance. A seeded RNG would not help here, because R’s Mersenne-Twister stream and NumPy’s are different streams: the same seed gives different draws, so any sampling step would break parity by construction. Determinism through absence is the only option that survives two languages, and it now extends to trial order, whose shuffle is described below.

anchor_pool <- pool[pool$frequency >= 5.2 & pool$frequency <= 7.0, ]
anchor_pool <- anchor_pool[
  order(anchor_pool$frequency, anchor_pool$word, method = "radix"),
]
idx <- unique(round(seq(1, nrow(anchor_pool), length.out = 15)))
idx
 [1]  1  7 13 19 25 31 37 44 50 56 62 68 74 80 86

The spread is seq() over the row positions, rounded to integers. Both engines compute the same positions from the same row count, and the rounding rule is written out in both.

Sorting is by byte order everywhere. R’s default string sort is locale-collated, and a French locale, a C locale and a Windows locale can order the same words differently, while any of those orders would differ from Python’s, which sorts by code point. Every sort on the selection path therefore passes method = "radix", which sorts by bytes.

words <- c("zebra", "Apple", "apple", "Zebra")
sort(words, method = "radix")
[1] "Apple" "Zebra" "apple" "zebra"

Uppercase sorts before lowercase because that is the byte order, and this is what Python’s sorted() produces. A locale-collated sort would typically interleave them. Case folding is pinned for the same reason: load_lexicon() lower-cases through ICU at the root locale rather than through tolower(), whose behaviour depends on the C library and the locale, and which differs from Python’s on Greek final sigma and the dotted Turkish capital I. The locale is kept out of two more places. Design, schema and registry files are read as UTF-8 whatever the session’s character type, and a file in another encoding is refused. The text of every hash key, behind the trial order, list balancing, jitter and the tie-break between candidates, is made UTF-8 before it is digested, whatever encoding mark it carries, so a condition label such as café ranks by the same digest in R under the C locale as in Python.

Frequencies of bigrams and of subsyllabic constituents are accumulated as integers, never as running floating-point sums, so the counts cannot depend on summation order.

Rounding comes before the tie-break, which is the subtle one of these mechanisms. Two candidate words can sit at exactly equal distance from an anchor, and the last bits of a square root can differ between two linear-algebra implementations. If the engines compared raw doubles, an inconsequential difference in the fifteenth decimal would make one engine call a tie and the other not, and they would pick different words. Distances are therefore rounded to nine decimal places before ranking, which puts both engines on the same side of every comparison that matters.

Rounding creates ties rather than removing them, so the ties in turn need a rule that both engines can apply identically, and that rule is a total order. Under tie_break: bytes, the rule of lexsync 0.1, candidates are ordered by distance, then by the word’s bytes, then by its integer id. That is the comparison the matcher makes, and it is reproduced here on three imaginary candidates.

distance <- c(0.5, 0.5, 0.2)
word     <- c("beta", "alpha", "gamma")
id       <- c(1L, 2L, 3L)
word[order(distance, word, id, method = "radix")]
[1] "gamma" "alpha" "beta"

gamma wins on distance. alpha and beta are tied on distance to the ninth decimal, and the word’s bytes settle it, identically in both engines. Since word is unique within a lexicon the order is total, so there is always exactly one winner and never a coin to flip.

Under tie_break: hash, the default, the word’s bytes give way to its tie key, the hexadecimal SHA-256 of lexsync-tie-v1| followed by the word. Both engines compute the key from the same UTF-8 bytes and sort it the same way. Here are four candidates tied on distance, in the order each rule gives them.

tied <- c("bat", "cat", "dog", "eel")
key <- vapply(paste0("lexsync-tie-v1|", tied), digest::digest, character(1),
              algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE, USE.NAMES = FALSE)
data.frame(bytes = tied[order(tied, method = "radix")],
           hash = tied[order(key, method = "radix")])
  bytes hash
1   bat  eel
2   cat  dog
3   dog  cat
4   eel  bat

Either rule is a total order that the two engines compute identically, so either keeps the guarantee, and the choice between them is a setting, matching.tie_break. bytes reproduces the selections of lexsync 0.1. hash, the default, stops a condition decided by ties from filling with early-alphabet words, which the matching vignette measures. Its salt is fixed and independent of the seed, which keys the trial order. A tie key built on the seed would change the items whenever a cohort’s order was re-randomised, and would let re-seeding shop among equally matched sets.

The even-spread rounding is shared as well. unique(round(seq(...))) is used identically in both engines, including the unique(), which matters when the pool is smaller than the requested n and the rounding produces a repeated index.

Trial order: a seeded shuffle without a generator

Trial order used to be the honest exception. Each engine drew the order from its own seeded generator, R’s Mersenne-Twister against NumPy’s PCG64, and the same seed could not give the same permutation, so an order was reproducible within an engine and different between the engines. That exception is retired. Order is now decided by a keyed hash: each row of a list is ranked by the SHA-256 digest of seed|replicate|list|set|condition, a tuple that identifies the trial uniquely under either counterbalancing recipe. Distinct inputs to SHA-256 behave as independent uniform draws, so sorting rows by their digests realises a seeded random permutation, and because a digest is a pure function of its input, the permutation is a pure function of the design: the same bytes from both engines on any platform, no generator state to save or restore, and a different order for every seed. The implementation is .shuffle_deterministic() in R/counterbalancing.R, mirrored in the Python engine’s counterbalancing.py.

stim <- counterbalance(match_stimuli(pool, design, schema), design, schema)
head(stim[, c("trial", "condition", "word")], 4)
  trial condition    word
1     1       low arrange
2     2      high    with
3     3      high  coming
4     4      high   major
same <- counterbalance(match_stimuli(pool, design, schema), design, schema)
identical(stim$trial, same$trial)
[1] TRUE

The order is still randomised in the sense a study needs: an item’s properties bear no systematic relation to its position, and a different seed gives a different order. What changed is that the permutation is engine-invariant, so it now sits inside the cross-engine contract, and the guarantee reaches the generated experiments whole: for every shipped design, the PsychoPy script, the OpenSesame file, the jsPsych page and the three CSV tables that the PsychoPy and OpenSesame experiments read are byte-identical across the engines.

One detail matters to anyone embedding lexsync in a longer script: counterbalancing no longer touches the random number generator at all, since nothing in the package consults one, so calling it cannot disturb the stream your own code is drawing from.

The CSV input contract

Both engines read a lexicon, a norm table, a supplied pool or an item table by one rule. Each reads every cell as text and converts it itself. readr and pandas guess types by different heuristics, and the guesses used to disagree: a padded category made the Python engine refuse a design this engine ran, and a column of T and F was written FALSE here and F there.

Header names and cells are trimmed of spaces, tabs, carriage returns and line feeds. After trimming, an empty cell and NA (quoted or not) are missing, and every other word is a value. A column is numeric only when every value is a plain decimal number, with an optional sign, point and exponent and no thousands separators, so 1,000 is text. It is logical only when every value is TRUE or FALSE in upper, lower or title case, so T and F stay text. Any other column is text, a column of dates included. Every row counts towards the type. The columns a paradigm presents, and an item table’s item and condition, are always text. A header that names a column twice is refused, and an empty header cell is named by its position (...3).

The numbers themselves are parsed to the same double in both engines. Python’s float() returns the double nearest the decimal. readr’s parser and R’s as.numeric() can each miss it by one unit in the last place, readr’s on 50.768212762897100 and as.numeric() on 0.586135918132, for instance. This engine therefore computes every number of up to 15 significant digits, with a power of ten within 10^22, as one exact integer multiplied or divided by one exact power of ten. IEEE-754 rounds that single operation correctly, so the result is Python’s double. Every value in the shipped lexica is of that kind. Any other number is rounded in exact integer arithmetic, which gives Python’s double on every platform. as.numeric() is not used there, because it accumulates the digits in long double. Where that type is no wider than a double, as on Apple Silicon, an emulation of R’s parser missed on about one in ten of the values Python’s repr() writes for computed doubles. A negative zero is read as zero, since the two engines would otherwise write it as -0 and 0.

The YAML input contract

A design and the schema are read as YAML 1.1, by yaml::read_yaml() here and by PyYAML in Python, and the two readers resolve a few unquoted values differently. YAML 1.1 lists y, Y, n and N among its booleans, and PyYAML keeps them as text. lexsync reads them as text in both engines, so keys: [y, n] gives the response keys y and n. Booleans are written true and false. An unquoted yes, no, on or off is a boolean to both readers as well. A response key that YAML reads as a boolean is therefore refused with a hint to quote it. A norms entry names its join key join_on, since a bare on is read as true. counterbalance.optimise must be true or false, and any other value, such as n or 1, is refused.

Some differences remain, and they are known. PyYAML reads 1:30 as the base-60 number 90, 1_000 as 1000, 0b101 as 5 and 2026-10-13 as a date, and this engine reads all four as text. No shipped design or schema holds such a value. Quote one, or write the number plainly, where a design must read alike in both engines. This engine also reads a sequence of one value, such as [true], as that value, while PyYAML keeps a list. optimise: [true] or name: [demo] therefore passes here and is refused in Python, so write a single value without brackets.

The Unicode input contract

Word matching, deduplication and the length dimension operate on Unicode code points, and every text key is normalised to Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC). The words of a lexicon or a supplied pool and both sides of a norm-table or pair-member join are first trimmed and lower-cased as described above. The item id, condition and presented fields of an item table, practice and filler tables included, and a supplied reference list are normalised as read. A precomposed character such as é and its decomposed counterpart, the base letter followed by a combining accent, are therefore one character, and a lexicon that mixes the two conventions holds each word once, in the first row the file gives it. Before this, the two spellings were two words of different lengths, and the matcher could place them in opposite conditions of one matched set. When normalisation rewrites or merges anything, the run log says how many forms it rewrote and how many duplicates it removed, and the datasheet records the two counts as materials_source$input_normalisation. Input already in NFC, the form most corpora distribute, leaves no trace.

Unicode’s stability policy fixes the NFC form of every assigned character, so the two engines can disagree only on a character that one engine’s Unicode version assigns and the other’s lacks. R’s stringi uses the ICU it bundles or, on some Linux builds, the system’s ICU, which may implement another version, and Python’s unicodedata follows the interpreter (Unicode 15.1 in Python 3.13).

The syllable estimator and the pseudoword generators carry a narrower contract still. Both are orthographic approximations defined for Latin orthographies. count_syllables() decomposes a word (NFD), sets its combining marks aside and counts the maximal runs of the letters a, e, i, o, u, y, ae (U+00E6), o with stroke (U+00F8), dotless i (U+0131) and oe (U+0153), so a vowel counts whatever its accent, in Polish, Czech, Hungarian, Romanian, Turkish and Vietnamese as in English or Spanish. Hiatus (idea counts 2) and the Czech syllabic r and l (vlk, krk) stay undercounted. A word holding a character outside the code points U+0001-U+024F, U+02B0-U+036F, U+1E00-U+1EFF and U+2000-U+206F gets no estimate. Its n_syllables is NA in R and NaN in Python, and run_pipeline() refuses a design that refers to n_syllables while its pool holds such a word. The test is on code-point ranges, which keeps the two engines independent of their Unicode tables, and the same stability policy fixes the decompositions. This vignette said before that the class covered the Latin-1 vowels, but it lacked U+00E6, and every Chinese, Russian or Greek word counted 0 syllables. The pseudoword generators build their candidates from lower-case a to z. The shipped Chinese design matches on length, n_density and old20 for these reasons.

File names

Every file a run writes is named after a stem built from the design’s name and language, which design_stem() computes in both engines. The stem keeps ASCII letters and digits only, so names that differ only outside ASCII would share it: two designs with Chinese names, both in chinese, would write the same files, the second overwriting the first. Whenever the name or the language holds a non-ASCII character, the stem therefore ends in an underscore and the first eight hexadecimal digits of the SHA-256 of the NFC-normalised text name|language, such as chinese_14aadfa7. A name and language with no ASCII letter or digit at all, which used to give file names beginning with an underscore or a dot, get those eight digits alone. Normalising to NFC here keeps a precomposed and a decomposed spelling of one name on one stem. Names in plain ASCII are unaffected. run_all() also computes every design’s stem before it runs any, and refuses two designs that would write the same files, such as en-lexdec and en_lexdec.

The documented exceptions

mahalanobis and optimal are equivalent to their byte-identical siblings in what they compute and not in what they select, and the reason is worth understanding.

mahalanobis needs the inverse of the pool’s correlation matrix. A matrix inverse is computed by LAPACK, and R’s LAPACK is not necessarily the one NumPy is built against. The two may differ in blocking, in vectorisation and in the order they accumulate sums. The results agree to well within any tolerance you would care about and they need not agree in their last bits, and the rounding that saves the Euclidean path cannot save this one: the distance is now a function of a matrix whose entries already differ below the rounding threshold, so the rounding can land on either side.

optimal solves a linear assignment problem. Where several assignments have the same total cost, which one a solver returns is an implementation detail of the solver, and R’s clue::solve_LSAP() and SciPy’s implementation resolve those ties differently. Both return an optimal assignment. They need not return the same one.

Neither is a bug that a determined engineer could fix. Guaranteeing them would mean shipping a bit-exact matrix inverse and a tie-canonical assignment solver in both languages, which is a large amount of numerical code to maintain for a modest gain. The chosen trade-off is to keep the byte-identical methods as the defaults, document the exception, and record it per run.

maha <- design
maha$matching <- list(method = "mahalanobis")
maha_stim <- match_stimuli(pool, maha, schema)
maha_ds <- build_datasheet(
  maha, schema, NULL, maha_stim,
  system.file("extdata", "en_example.csv", package = "lexsync"),
  list(stimuli = NA_character_), schema$seed
)
maha_ds$selection$cross_engine
[1] "approximate (platform linear algebra)"

Every datasheet carries this field, so a reader of the record does not have to know the rule. It reads byte-identical for the default methods and approximate (platform linear algebra) for these two, and the generated methods paragraph adds a sentence stating the caveat in prose when it applies. The constraint also shapes the roadmap: a covariance-aware distance might well be the better default, and it stays optional precisely because it cannot carry the guarantee.

One further place is worth naming, though it is not an exception. Almost everything on the path to a compared artefact is built from operations IEEE-754 either mandates correctly rounded or makes exact, so the engines agree by construction rather than by measurement. The Student t quantile and distribution behind the confidence interval and the TOST p-value are where that argument does not reach: stats::qt and stats::pt on one side, SciPy’s on the other, two independent implementations that were measured to disagree by up to about 1e-12 over the range these reports use. The published values are rounded to three and four decimal places, which leaves 5e-4 and 5e-5 of headroom, so the comparisons files still come out byte-identical. The guarantee there rests on a margin of some seven orders of magnitude rather than on the construction, and saying so is what stops anyone widening the reported precision without checking the margin first.

normalise_lexicon() has the same kind of step. Zipf = log10(per million) + 3 calls each engine’s own log10(), which IEEE-754 does not require to be correctly rounded. A value whose scaled Zipf lies within one unit in the last place of a rounding boundary could therefore round to different three-place values in the two engines. The function counts the values that lie within 1e-9 of a boundary, and the count is expected to be 0. A run over a lexicon carrying freq_permillion records it as materials_source$zipf_derivation in its datasheet and in its run log. A registry entry’s derived file, a lexicon normalised once and checksummed, lets both engines read the same bytes and leaves no such step at all.

The parity test

A guarantee that is not tested is a comment. The parity gate in continuous integration runs the R pipeline over the shipped designs, regenerates each with the Python engine and compares the two, across designs covering both engines’ matching methods, continuous selection, both pseudoword generators, resampling, priming and self-paced reading, three languages including a logographic script, and three reproductions of published designs.

The comparison is on identity columns: the word or target, the condition and the set index. Including set is what gives the test teeth, since without it the engines could select the same items and pair them differently and still pass. Having matched on those, the test then checks every other shared column, so the trial position and the dimensions each engine computes at run time (n_density, old20, n_syllables, bigram_freq) must also agree.

Three details keep the gate from passing vacuously. The test skips when the R reference output is absent, since the Python package can be installed on its own, so CI sets LEXSYNC_REQUIRE_PARITY=1 to turn those skips into failures: a job meant to run both engines cannot pass by quietly skipping. The R references are regenerated and then checked with git diff --exit-code, so an R-engine regression fails the build. Without that step the comparison would run against a stale snapshot that the regression matches. And the R suite is run once from the source tree with a check that nothing skipped, because the repository-coupled tests silently skip when run from an installed copy.

The shipped designs have clean inputs: every cell is in NFC, none is padded and the norms cover every word. The gate therefore never reaches the code that padded fields, missing values or unusual YAML would take, and a defect both engines share would pass it, since they agree. The twin-edge cases cover that ground. Each is a folder under parity/twin_edge/ at the repository root, holding a small design.yaml, its inputs (paths relative to the folder), an optional schema.yaml and an expect.yaml that pins the outcome. An artefacts case keeps the files the design must produce, byte for byte, in expected/, and may assert values in the datasheet. A refusal case gives a substring of the error the design must raise. The R suite’s test-twin-edge.R and the Python suite’s test_twin_edge.py each hold their own engine to every case. CI also runs tools/compare_engines.py, which compares the two engines on the same cases and repeats the whole-tree comparison on any machine. To add a case, create its folder with design.yaml and expect.yaml and write expected/ with python tools/twin_edge.py --update <case>. Read the pinned files to confirm they are right, then run this suite, which checks that the R engine writes the same bytes. A fix for an input defect adds its case in the same commit, so the gate never lands red.

The materials datasheet

Each run emits a datasheet in two forms, a JSON record for machines and a Markdown rendering for people. It exists because the reproducibility literature in linguistics keeps finding the same gap: materials are described but rarely deposited in a form that permits reuse or verification (Bochynska et al., 2023), and the degrees of freedom in preparing them are large enough to matter (Roettger, 2019). A datasheet is the FAIR-style record of one selection (Wilkinson et al., 2016).

out <- file.path(tempdir(), "lexsync_repro")
dir.create(out, showWarnings = FALSE)
report <- match_report(
  stim, c("frequency", "length", "n_density", "old20"), schema
)
stim_path <- file.path(out, "stimuli.csv")
write.csv(stim, stim_path, row.names = FALSE)

ds <- build_datasheet(
  design, schema, report, stim,
  source_path = system.file("extdata", "en_example.csv", package = "lexsync"),
  artifacts = list(stimuli = stim_path),
  seed = schema$seed,
  candidate_pool = lapply(design$conditions, function(cnd)
    list(
      condition = cnd$name,
      n_candidates = nrow(build_pool(pool, cnd$define_by))
    ))
)
names(ds)
 [1] "lexsync_datasheet_version" "design"                   
 [3] "materials_source"          "dimensions"               
 [5] "selection"                 "relational"               
 [7] "analysis"                  "equivalence"              
 [9] "realised_control"          "counterbalancing"         
[11] "presentation"              "resampling"               
[13] "items"                     "reproducibility"          
[15] "artifacts"

The record answers the questions a sceptical reader would ask. Where the words came from, and whether this is the same file, is settled by materials_source, which carries the path and its SHA-256. What was applied is recorded in selection, covering the method, the matched dimensions and the tolerance windows as resolved, which is the design’s overrides merged onto the schema’s defaults rather than the defaults a design may have replaced. The rule that broke exact ties is there too, as tie_break, with its salt under hash. What the selection achieved is in realised_control, as the effect sizes, intervals, variance ratios and TOST verdicts for every pair of conditions, each row naming its pair in condition and reference, giving the raw difference as mean_diff and the dimension’s role. What it could have chosen instead is in candidate_pool, which records how many items satisfied each condition before matching. A candidate missing a matched dimension satisfies its condition but cannot be matched. Such candidates are counted in incomplete_dropped, present only when a condition lost any, and the methods paragraph leaves them out of its count of eligible candidates. How the items were dealt to lists is in counterbalancing. It gives the recipe that ran, the lists the stimuli table holds and the trials each list gives each condition, and it says whether a Latin-square rotation is complete. How many items there are is in items, whose n_per_condition_realised counts the items each condition holds, per replicate for resampled sets. The request the selector applied is design$n_per_condition, its default when the design gives none.

The record keeps each statistic as the comparisons report rounded it, to three places and the TOST p to four. The Markdown rendering and the methods paragraph show them at two or three places and the TOST p at four. The rounding is done by lexsync’s own formatter, half away from zero from that record, so both engines print the same digits. A d of 0.1649 is stored as 0.165 and is therefore shown as 0.17.

ds$materials_source$sha256
[1] "34a3c81cb559a42918864f5ecd2bcea93647cc4b0058dd03132ffe8723f4c310"
str(ds$selection$tolerance_k)
List of 4
 $ length   : num 2
 $ frequency: num 1
 $ n_density: num 2
 $ old20    : num 2
do.call(rbind, lapply(ds$selection$candidate_pool, as.data.frame))
  condition n_candidates
1      high           86
2       low          465

The candidate-pool counts do a job that is easy to miss. Here the high condition was drawn from fewer than a hundred eligible words and the low condition from several hundred, which are different epistemic situations: choosing 15 items from a large candidate set invites the concern that a selection could be steered towards almost any result, whereas a condition with barely more candidates than items had little freedom to be steered. Recording the counts, alongside the fact that the selection is deterministic and blind to any outcome measure, lets a reader judge that rather than take it on trust.

Note that the resolved windows include a frequency entry even though this design matches on the three orthographic dimensions only. The record reports the windows as resolved from the schema and the design, and a window is applied only to a dimension named in match_on.

str(ds$reproducibility)
List of 2
 $ seed    : int 2026
 $ versions:List of 10
  ..$ engine    : chr "R"
  ..$ lexsync   : chr "0.1.1"
  ..$ R         : chr "4.6.1"
  ..$ readr     : chr "2.2.0"
  ..$ stringdist: chr "0.9.17"
  ..$ jsonlite  : chr "2.0.0"
  ..$ digest    : chr "0.6.39"
  ..$ yaml      : chr "2.3.12"
  ..$ stringi   : chr "1.8.9"
  ..$ os        : chr "Linux x86_64"

The reproducibility block records the seed and the versions of the engine and its dependencies, since a bug fix in a dependency can change a selection and the record should say which versions produced this one.

The methods paragraph and the pre-registration template

The datasheet renders itself into prose, which is a small feature that removes a common source of error: a methods section transcribed by hand from numbers on a screen.

cat(strwrap(methods_paragraph(ds), width = 76), sep = "\n")
15 items per condition were selected from the English lexicon (wordfreq
(Speer, 2022) screened against SUBTLEX-US (Brysbaert & New, 2009), data CC
BY-SA 4.0; forms absent from SUBTLEX-US or beginning with a lower-case
letter in under 10% of their uses are left out, and N and OLD20 count
neighbours only among the forms the screen keeps; full corpus licence and
citation at
https://github.com/pablobernabeu/lexsync/blob/main/corpora/ATTRIBUTION.md)
and matched item by item on length, n_density, old20 using lexsync's
standardised_euclidean matcher. The largest difference on a matched
dimension was -0.133 neighbours in n_density (low against high; d = -0.03,
90% CI [-0.66, 0.59]). Two one-sided tests at a bound of 0.5 SD (alpha
0.05) supported equivalence on 0 of 3 matched comparisons; with 15 items
per condition no dimension that varies can pass this test, however well
matched. The smallest condition was selected from 86 eligible candidates,
and the selection was deterministic and blind to any outcome measure.
Materials were counterbalanced into 1 list(s) (a factorial split) and
generated for PsychoPy, OpenSesame and jsPsych. Responses were collected
from target onset until 2800 ms after it, and a response ended the trial.
The selection is deterministic and reproducible (lexsync 0.1.1), and the
seed (2026) fixes the trial order.

The paragraph is generated from the record, so it cannot disagree with the stimuli. It states the items each condition holds and the candidate-pool size, and it adds the cross-engine caveat when the design’s method warrants it. It describes the realised control before it tests it, since tests on a selected set concern a closed population (Sassenhagen & Alday, 2016). It gives the largest difference on any matched dimension, in that dimension’s unit, with d and its interval, and only then the two one-sided tests, with the number of matched comparisons they supported. It then names, largest first, up to five comparisons of a dimension the design did not control whose |d| exceeds the equivalence bound. The report here covers only the matched dimensions and frequency, which defines the conditions, so there is none to name.

This run shows why the order matters, and why the paragraph is a draft to adapt rather than one to paste unread. The demonstration matches only 15 items per condition. At a bound of 0.5 SD and an alpha of .05, no dimension that varies can pass the tests with fewer than 23 items per condition, however well it is matched. The paragraph says so, and a failed test is then not mistaken for a failed match. That is the dependence on set size that the matching vignette warns against reading past. A real study would either match enough items or report the control by the differences it describes.

write_datasheet() writes both forms, and the Markdown rendering carries a pre-registration skeleton with its materials section already filled in.

paths <- write_datasheet(
  ds, file.path(out, "datasheet.json"), file.path(out, "datasheet.md")
)
md <- readLines(file.path(out, "datasheet.md"))
grep("^#", md, value = TRUE)
 [1] "# Materials datasheet -- vignette_repro (english)"
 [2] "## Provenance"                                    
 [3] "## Counterbalanced lists"                         
 [4] "## Selection transparency"                        
 [5] "## Realised control"                              
 [6] "## Suggested analysis"                            
 [7] "## Methods paragraph"                             
 [8] "## Pre-registration template"                     
 [9] "### Study information"                            
[10] "### Hypotheses"                                   
[11] "### Design"                                       
[12] "### Materials (from the lexsync datasheet)"       
[13] "### Sampling plan"                                
[14] "### Analysis plan"

The sections left blank are the ones no tool can fill: the hypotheses, the sampling plan and the inference criteria. The analysis plan is the exception: it arrives with a suggested model, and the suggestion takes a position.

ds$analysis$suggested_model
[1] "response ~ condition + scale(length, scale = FALSE) + scale(n_density, scale = FALSE) + scale(old20, scale = FALSE) + (1 + condition | subject) + (1 | item)"

The model crosses random effects for subjects and items because items are a sample of the language rather than the population of interest, and an analysis treating them as fixed generalises only to the words that were used (Clark, 1973; Yarkoni, 2022). The matched dimensions enter as centred covariates, computed from the stimuli file’s own columns, because matching leaves residual differences and Sassenhagen and Alday (2016) recommend adjusting for potential confounds. A structure is maximal only when every effect that varies within subjects or items has a random slope there (Barr et al., 2013). These covariates have none, so the accompanying note describes the slopes the model has. It also advises simplifying a model that is singular or fails to converge (Matuschek et al., 2017). It is a starting point for a design of this shape.

The run log

The datasheet records what a run produced. The run log records what it did.

log <- new_run_log(
  "vignette_repro",
  meta = list(seed = schema$seed, language = "english")
)
log <- log_step(
  log,
  sprintf("lexicon loaded: %d words", nrow(lex)),
  list(words = nrow(lex))
)
[lexsync] lexicon loaded: 3000 words
log <- log_step(log, sprintf("pool after filters: %d words", nrow(pool)))
[lexsync] pool after filters: 859 words
log <- log_artefact(log, stim_path, rows = nrow(stim))
[lexsync] wrote 'stimuli.csv'
log_md <- write_run_log(log, file.path(out, "run_log.md"),
                        file.path(out, "run_log.jsonl"))
cat(readLines(log_md), sep = "\n")
# lexsync run log: vignette_repro

- Engine: R 4.6.1
- Started: 2026-10-16 22:38:14.033363
- Finished: 2026-10-16 22:38:14.035492

## Run metadata

- seed: 2026
- language: english

## Steps

- **2026-10-16 22:38:14.034113**: lexicon loaded: 3000 words
    - words: 3000
- **2026-10-16 22:38:14.034515**: pool after filters: 859 words
- **2026-10-16 22:38:14.034883**: wrote 'stimuli.csv'
    - path: /tmp/RtmpTeMgfB/lexsync_repro/stimuli.csv
    - rows: 30
    - md5: 06832f9e8e1d901adde134e464579401

The pipeline builds this log as it goes, recording each stage with its parameters, the equivalence verdict on every dimension, any balance warning, and an entry per file written with its MD5. The experiments’ loop and text tables are among them, and the stimuli and report tables are logged with their row counts too. A design or schema key that lexsync does not read is noted there as well, since it changed nothing about the run. Both a Markdown log and a JSON Lines log are emitted, the latter so that a run can be checked by a script. The MD5 here is a content fingerprint for spotting drift between runs, whereas the datasheet’s SHA-256 is the stronger one that belongs in a permanent record.

Reproducing a run

The pipeline does all of the above in one call, and run_pipeline() on a design configuration is the reproducible unit: it writes the stimuli, the reports, the three experiments, the datasheet and the log. Sharing the design file and the corpus is then enough for someone else to regenerate the materials and verify the checksums, in either language.

Two habits make that work. Pin the corpus, since a selection is only reproducible against a fixed lexicon, which is why the bundled corpora are a checksummed snapshot and why the wordfreq connector draws on a package frozen in 2024, whose data is a stable snapshot of usage through roughly 2021. And where cross-engine reproducibility matters, prefer the default matching methods, since they are the ones that carry the guarantee.

A reproducible lexicon is not a screened one. The bundled lexica are the most frequent forms wordfreq returns, so they hold proper names, acronyms and other forms that are not words of the language, and N and OLD20 are computed over them. Their share differs between frequency bands, which can confound a frequency contrast. The repository’s corpora/derived/en_v2.csv marks such forms in the English lexicon, and What the derived lexica contain says what to check in a selection.
